EDUCATION
SEMESTER I & II
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

Educational psychology is the application of psychological knowledge to education. It helps teachers understand learners, learning, development, motivation, intelligence, personality and classroom behaviour.

Skinner defined educational psychology as the branch of psychology which deals with teaching and learning. Crow and Crow described it as the study of the learning experiences of an individual from birth to old age. It is an applied, positive science that uses scientific methods such as observation, experiment, case study and survey.

Its scope includes the learner (growth, development, individual differences, intelligence, personality), the learning process (theories, motivation, memory, transfer of learning), the learning situation (classroom climate, discipline, teaching aids) and the teacher (teaching methods, mental health, evaluation).
Educational psychology helps teachers understand individual differences, choose suitable teaching methods, motivate learners, manage classrooms and evaluate learning more effectively.

For the teacher: it helps in knowing the learner's abilities, interests and needs; selecting suitable methods and teaching aids; motivating students; maintaining discipline; dealing with problem children; and guiding students in educational and vocational choices.

It also helps in framing the curriculum according to the developmental stage, in measuring and evaluating learning through tests, in providing special education for gifted and backward children, and in maintaining the mental health of both teacher and pupils.

Growth mainly refers to quantitative changes such as height and weight, while development includes wider qualitative and quantitative changes. Development follows an orderly pattern and is influenced by heredity and environment.

Differences: growth is quantitative (increase in size and weight), development is both quantitative and qualitative (including emotional, social and intellectual changes); growth stops at maturity, while development continues throughout life; growth can be measured directly, development is observed through behaviour.

Principles of development: it is continuous; it follows a pattern (cephalocaudal - head to toe, and proximodistal - centre to outward); it proceeds from general to specific; it is the result of interaction between heredity and environment; and individuals differ in their rate of development. These principles help teachers plan activities suited to each stage.

Adolescence involves major physical, social and intellectual changes. Physical maturity increases, social relationships become more important and the capacity for reasoning and independent thinking develops.

Stanley Hall described adolescence (roughly 12-19 years) as a period of 'storm and stress'. Physical changes include a growth spurt, puberty and development of secondary sexual characteristics. Emotional changes include mood swings, sensitivity, anxiety and a search for identity (Erikson's identity versus role confusion).

Intellectually, adolescents develop abstract reasoning (Piaget's formal operational stage), imagination and critical thinking. Socially, peer groups become important and the desire for independence increases. Educational implications: guidance and counselling, sex education, co-curricular activities, respect for their opinions, and positive role models.
Intelligence is the ability to learn, understand, reason, solve problems and adjust effectively. Individuals differ in the level and pattern of intellectual abilities.

Definitions: Binet - the ability to judge well, understand well and reason well; Terman - the ability to carry on abstract thinking; Wechsler - the aggregate or global capacity of the individual to act purposefully, think rationally and deal effectively with the environment.

Intelligence is measured by intelligence tests and expressed as IQ = (Mental Age / Chronological Age) x 100. Tests may be verbal or non-verbal and individual or group. Classification: IQ above 140 is genius, 90-110 is average, and below 70 indicates intellectual disability. Theories include Spearman's two-factor, Thurstone's group-factor, Guilford's structure of intellect and Gardner's multiple intelligences.
Creativity is the ability to produce original and useful ideas or solutions. It involves imagination, flexibility and originality.

Characteristics of creativity: originality (new ideas), fluency (many ideas), flexibility (different types of ideas) and elaboration (developing ideas in detail). J.P. Guilford linked creativity to divergent thinking, which produces many possible answers, as opposed to convergent thinking, which finds one correct answer.

Stages of the creative process (Graham Wallas): preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. Creative children are curious, imaginative, independent, open to experience and willing to take risks.
Spearman proposed that intelligence contains a general factor, called 'g', common to intellectual activities, and specific factors, called 's', required for particular tasks.

Charles Spearman (1904) used factor analysis and found that all mental tasks share a general factor 'g' and each task also requires a specific factor 's'. 'g' is inborn, universal and constant, while 's' factors vary from task to task and can be developed by training.

Educational implication: a child with high 'g' tends to do well in all subjects, while 's' explains why a child may be especially good in music or mathematics. Criticism: it oversimplifies intelligence and ignores group factors.
Thurstone explained intelligence through several Primary Mental Abilities rather than one single general ability.

L.L. Thurstone (1938) proposed seven Primary Mental Abilities: (1) verbal comprehension, (2) word fluency, (3) number ability, (4) spatial ability, (5) memory, (6) perceptual speed and (7) reasoning. Intelligence is the combination of these relatively independent abilities.

This group-factor theory is useful in education because it suggests that students may have different profiles of strengths and weaknesses, which can guide subject choice and vocational guidance. Thurstone's Primary Mental Abilities test was based on this theory.
Education can promote creativity by encouraging questioning, imagination, independent thinking, problem-solving and freedom to express new ideas.

Ways to foster creativity: encouraging questions and curiosity, using open-ended questions and problem-solving tasks, brainstorming, providing freedom and a non-threatening classroom, appreciating original ideas, using activities like art, drama, music and projects, and avoiding over-emphasis on rote memorisation and examinations.

The teacher should be a creative role model, tolerate unusual answers, give time for incubation of ideas and provide opportunities for co-curricular activities. NEP 2020 emphasises creativity, critical thinking and experiential learning.
Intelligence is mainly connected with learning, reasoning and problem-solving, while creativity emphasizes originality and production of new ideas. They are related but not identical.

Research by Getzels and Jackson (1962) and Torrance found that intelligence and creativity are related but distinct; a person with high IQ may not be highly creative. The threshold theory suggests that a certain minimum level of intelligence (around IQ 120) is necessary for creativity, but above that level they are largely independent.
Intelligence tests measure convergent thinking; creativity tests (such as Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking) measure divergent thinking. Teachers should identify and nurture both.
Personality is the organised pattern of an individual's behaviour, feelings, attitudes and characteristics that makes the person distinctive.

The word personality comes from the Latin word 'persona', meaning a mask worn by actors. Gordon Allport defined personality as 'the dynamic organisation within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his unique adjustments to his environment'.

Characteristics: personality is unique, dynamic, consistent, the product of heredity and environment, and includes physical, mental, emotional and social aspects. A well-integrated personality is balanced, adjustable, socially responsible and emotionally mature.
The type approach groups people into broad personality categories according to common characteristics.

Examples: Hippocrates classified people by body fluids into sanguine (cheerful), choleric (irritable), melancholic (sad) and phlegmatic (calm). Kretschmer classified by body build into pyknic (short, round, sociable), asthenic (thin, reserved) and athletic. Sheldon classified into endomorph, mesomorph and ectomorph. Carl Jung classified people as introverts, extroverts and ambiverts.
Criticism: typologies oversimplify personality, as most people do not fit neatly into one type and may show features of several types.
The trait approach explains personality through relatively stable characteristics or traits that differ from one individual to another.

A trait is a relatively enduring characteristic such as honesty, sociability or anxiety. Gordon Allport classified traits into cardinal, central and secondary traits. Raymond Cattell identified 16 source traits (16 PF questionnaire). Eysenck proposed three dimensions: extraversion-introversion, neuroticism-stability and psychoticism.

The Big Five model (McCrae and Costa) includes openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism (OCEAN). The trait approach allows measurement of personality through rating scales and inventories.
The Rorschach test is a projective personality assessment in which a person interprets ambiguous inkblot figures. Responses are used to study aspects of personality.

The test was developed by Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach in 1921. It consists of 10 cards with inkblots - five black and grey, two black and red, and three multi-coloured. The person is asked what they see in each blot.

Responses are scored for location (whole or part of the blot), determinants (form, colour, shading, movement), content (human, animal, object) and popularity or originality. It reveals hidden aspects of personality, emotions and thought processes. Its limitations are subjective scoring and the need for trained experts.
The TAT is a projective test in which a person tells stories about ambiguous pictures. The stories are used to understand motives, feelings and personality tendencies.

The TAT was developed by Henry Murray and Christiana Morgan in 1935. It has 30 picture cards and one blank card; usually about 20 are shown. The person is asked to tell a story about what is happening, what led to it, what the characters feel and how it will end.

The stories are analysed to identify the person's needs (such as achievement, affiliation, power), conflicts and attitudes, based on Murray's theory of needs and press. Children's Apperception Test (CAT) is a version for children.
Personality development is influenced by heredity, family, school, culture, peer group, social environment and individual experiences.

Biological factors: heredity, physique, health and the endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal, pituitary) affect energy, emotions and growth. Psychological factors: intelligence, emotions, motivation and self-concept.

Social and cultural factors: family environment and parenting style, birth order, school and teachers, peer group, community, religion, mass media and culture. Educational implication: schools should provide a healthy environment, guidance, co-curricular activities and good role models for balanced personality development.
Learning is a relatively lasting change in behaviour, knowledge or skill resulting from experience and practice.

Definitions: Woodworth - any activity can be called learning so far as it develops the individual and makes his behaviour and experiences different from what they would otherwise have been; Gates - learning is the modification of behaviour through experience and training.

Characteristics: learning is continuous, purposive, goal-directed, results from experience, involves adjustment and is transferable. Changes due to maturation, fatigue or drugs are not learning. Types include motor learning, verbal learning, concept learning, problem-solving and attitude learning.
Learning is influenced by motivation, intelligence, interest, readiness, health, teaching method, practice and the learning environment.

Factors related to the learner: physical and mental health, maturation, intelligence, motivation, interest, attitude, aptitude and previous learning. Factors related to the teacher: knowledge of subject, teaching methods, personality and teacher-pupil relationship.

Factors related to the content and environment: difficulty and meaningfulness of material, organisation of curriculum, use of teaching aids, classroom environment, school climate and home environment. Methods such as practice, feedback, reinforcement and spaced learning improve retention.
Thorndike explained learning through connections between stimulus and response. His major laws include readiness, exercise and effect.

Edward L. Thorndike's experiment with a hungry cat in a puzzle box showed that the cat learned to open the box by trial and error; unsuccessful responses were gradually eliminated and the successful response was 'stamped in'. Hence the theory is also called trial-and-error learning or connectionism.

Primary laws: (1) law of readiness - learning occurs when the learner is ready; (2) law of exercise - practice strengthens connections (law of use and disuse); (3) law of effect - satisfying results strengthen and annoying results weaken connections. Educational implications: motivate students, provide practice and drill, give rewards and immediate feedback.
Skinner's operant conditioning explains learning through consequences. Behaviour followed by reinforcement is more likely to be repeated.

B.F. Skinner experimented with rats and pigeons in the 'Skinner box'. When the rat pressed a lever, it received food, which reinforced the behaviour. Behaviour that is followed by reinforcement is strengthened. Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus; negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant one; punishment reduces behaviour.

Schedules of reinforcement include continuous and partial (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval). Educational implications: programmed instruction, teaching machines, shaping of behaviour step by step, immediate feedback and the use of praise and rewards in the classroom.
Motivation is the force that starts, directs and sustains learning activity. It encourages attention, effort, persistence and achievement.

Types: intrinsic motivation comes from within (interest, curiosity, desire to learn), while extrinsic motivation comes from outside (marks, prizes, praise, punishment). Intrinsic motivation is more lasting. Maslow's hierarchy of needs (physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualisation) explains motivation.

Techniques for teachers: arousing interest and curiosity, setting clear goals, using praise and rewards, giving knowledge of results, encouraging healthy competition and cooperation, using teaching aids, relating lessons to life and creating a supportive classroom climate.

Educational psychology combines knowledge of psychology with educational practice. It studies learners and the learning process and helps teachers understand behaviour, individual differences, motivation and development.

Growth and development are important in education because teaching should suit the learner's stage of maturity. Growth often refers to measurable physical changes, while development is broader. During adolescence, learners experience rapid physical changes, changing social relationships and increasing intellectual ability.

A teacher who understands these changes can select suitable methods, provide guidance and create a better learning environment.

Meaning and nature: Educational psychology is the application of psychological principles to teaching and learning. It is an applied, positive and developing science that studies the behaviour of the learner in educational situations using methods like observation, experiment and case study.

Scope and implications: It covers the learner, the learning process, the learning situation and the teacher. It helps teachers understand individual differences, select methods, motivate learners, maintain discipline, guide pupils and evaluate learning.

Growth and development: Growth is physical and quantitative; development is total and qualitative. Development is continuous, follows a definite pattern, proceeds from general to specific and is influenced by heredity and environment. Stages include infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood.

Adolescence: Adolescence brings rapid physical growth, emotional instability, abstract thinking, peer influence and identity formation. Teachers should provide guidance and counselling, sex education, opportunities for self-expression and responsibility, and co-curricular activities to help adolescents develop a balanced personality.

Intelligence includes the ability to learn, reason, solve problems and adjust to new situations. Spearman explained intelligence through a general factor and specific factors, while Thurstone emphasized several Primary Mental Abilities.

Creativity is the capacity to produce original and useful ideas. Education can develop creativity by encouraging questioning, imagination, experimentation and independent thinking.

Intelligence and creativity are different. A learner may be intellectually capable without always being highly creative. Good education should therefore develop both reasoning ability and originality.
Meaning of intelligence: Intelligence is the general capacity to learn, think abstractly, solve problems and adapt to new situations. It is measured by IQ tests; IQ = MA/CA x 100.

Theories: Spearman's two-factor theory (general 'g' and specific 's' factors); Thurstone's theory of seven primary mental abilities; Guilford's structure of intellect model (operations, contents, products); Gardner's multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic).

Creativity: Creativity is the ability to produce novel and useful ideas, involving fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration. It depends on divergent thinking and passes through preparation, incubation, illumination and verification.

Relationship and role of education: Intelligence and creativity are related but not identical; high intelligence does not guarantee creativity. Education can foster both through stimulating environments, open-ended tasks, freedom of expression, encouragement of curiosity, project work and recognition of original ideas, rather than relying only on memorisation.

Personality refers to the organised characteristics, behaviour and emotional patterns of an individual. The type approach places individuals into broad categories, while the trait approach studies relatively stable characteristics.

Personality can be assessed through different methods. The syllabus includes the Rorschach Ink-blot Test and Thematic Apperception Test as projective techniques. Personality is influenced by heredity as well as family, school, culture, peers and personal experiences.

Education contributes to personality development by providing social experience, discipline, opportunities for expression and healthy relationships.
Meaning: Personality is the dynamic organisation of an individual's physical, mental, emotional and social traits that determines their unique adjustment to the environment (Allport).

Approaches: The type approach classifies people into categories - Hippocrates (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic), Kretschmer, Sheldon and Jung (introvert and extrovert). The trait approach describes personality by measurable traits - Allport's cardinal, central and secondary traits, Cattell's 16 factors, Eysenck's dimensions and the Big Five.

Assessment: Personality is assessed by subjective methods (interview, autobiography), objective methods (observation, rating scales, personality inventories) and projective techniques. The Rorschach Ink-blot Test uses ten inkblots, and the TAT uses ambiguous pictures to bring out hidden motives and conflicts.

Factors affecting personality: Heredity, physique, glands, intelligence, family, school, peer group, culture and mass media. The school can promote a balanced personality through a healthy environment, guidance, co-curricular activities and value education.

Learning is a relatively lasting change produced through experience and practice. It is affected by motivation, readiness, intelligence, interest, health, teaching methods and environment.

Thorndike explained learning through stimulus-response connections and laws such as readiness, exercise and effect. Skinner emphasized operant conditioning, where reinforcement strengthens behaviour.

Motivation gives direction and energy to learning. A motivated learner is more likely to pay attention, make effort and continue working despite difficulty.

Learning: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience and practice. It is influenced by the learner's maturation, motivation, intelligence and health, by the teacher's methods, by the nature of content and by the environment.

Thorndike's connectionism: Based on the puzzle-box experiment with a cat, learning occurs by trial and error. The laws of readiness, exercise and effect have educational implications such as motivation, practice and rewards.

Skinner's operant conditioning: Behaviour is shaped by its consequences; reinforced behaviour is repeated. Schedules of reinforcement, shaping and programmed learning are its applications in education.

Motivation: Motivation energises and directs learning. Intrinsic motivation (interest, curiosity) is more effective than extrinsic motivation (rewards, punishment). Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains that basic needs must be met before higher learning goals. Teachers motivate pupils through interest, goals, praise, feedback, competition and cooperation.
Sociology studies society and social relationships. Education is a social process and is closely related to family, culture, institutions and social change.
The term 'sociology' was coined by Auguste Comte, who is regarded as the father of sociology. Sociology studies social groups, institutions, interaction, social change and social problems.

Education is a social process because it takes place in society, is shaped by society's needs and values, and in turn shapes society. Durkheim described education as the methodical socialisation of the younger generation.
Educational Sociology applies sociological ideas to education. It studies education in relation to society, groups, culture, socialisation, mobility and change.

Educational sociology, developed by thinkers such as Durkheim, Dewey and Lester Ward, studies the interaction between education and society. A related field, sociology of education, studies education as a social institution more objectively.

Its scope includes the relationship between education and social institutions (family, religion, economy, polity), socialisation, social change, social stratification and mobility, culture, community and the school as a social organisation.
A sociological approach helps teachers understand the social background of learners, group behaviour, inequality, culture and the role of education in society.

The sociological approach is needed because the child is a social being, and education aims at social efficiency and adjustment. It helps teachers understand social influences on learning, such as family background, caste, class and community, and helps reduce inequality.

It also helps in framing curriculum according to social needs, promoting democratic values, national integration and social change, and dealing with social problems such as poverty, gender discrimination and drug abuse.
Society is a network of social relationships among people. It includes individuals, groups, institutions, norms and shared ways of life and performs functions necessary for social life.

MacIver and Page defined society as a 'web of social relationships'. Features of society include likeness and difference, interdependence, cooperation and conflict, permanence, social control and culture.

Society has various institutions - family, education, religion, economy and government - each fulfilling important functions. Education is one of the most important institutions because it preserves and transmits culture.
Socialization is the process through which individuals learn the values, norms, behaviour and roles of society.
Socialisation is a lifelong process that transforms a biological individual into a social being. Through it, a child learns language, customs, roles, values and expected behaviour.

Theories: Cooley's 'looking-glass self' (we see ourselves as others see us), G.H. Mead's development of the self through role-taking ('I' and 'me'), Freud's psychoanalytic view and Piaget's moral development. Socialisation may be primary (in the family) or secondary (school, workplace, media).
Family, school, community and peer group are major agencies of socialization. Each influences behaviour, attitudes and social development.

Family: the first and most important agency; it teaches language, habits, values and emotional security. School: teaches knowledge, discipline, cooperation and social roles through formal education and co-curricular activities. Community: provides wider social experience, customs and traditions; in Mizoram, the YMA and church play a large role.

Peer group: friends of the same age influence attitudes, interests and behaviour, especially in adolescence. Other agencies include religion, mass media and social media, which have become very influential.
Primary groups are small and based on close personal relationships, while secondary groups are larger and more formal and goal-oriented.

The concept of primary group was given by Charles Horton Cooley. Primary groups (family, play group, neighbourhood) are characterised by face-to-face relations, small size, intimacy, permanence and a 'we-feeling'. They shape personality and values.

Secondary groups (political parties, trade unions, universities, clubs) are larger, formal, impersonal, and formed for specific purposes. In modern society the importance of secondary groups has increased. Both types play roles in education.
Social control refers to the ways society regulates behaviour. Education promotes social control by teaching values, discipline, rules and responsible behaviour.

Social control may be formal (laws, police, courts, rules of institutions) or informal (customs, traditions, folkways, mores, religion, public opinion). E.A. Ross wrote a famous book on social control (1901).

Education acts as an agency of social control by teaching norms and values, developing self-discipline, respect for law and a sense of responsibility, and by promoting critical thinking so that control is not blind obedience. School rules, co-curricular activities and teachers' example contribute to this.
Social stratification is the division of society into unequal social layers or categories. Education can sometimes reflect social inequalities and can also influence a person's social position.
Stratification may be based on caste, class, gender, race, ethnicity, wealth, power and education. Caste is a closed system (membership by birth), while class is an open system (mobility possible).

Education can reproduce inequality when good schools are available only to the rich, but it can also reduce inequality by providing equal opportunities. Constitutional provisions such as reservation, free and compulsory education (RTE Act) and scholarships aim at equalising educational opportunities.
Social mobility means movement from one social position to another. Education can promote mobility by providing knowledge, qualifications and opportunities.

Types: vertical mobility (upward or downward), horizontal mobility (change of occupation without change in status), intergenerational (between parents and children) and intragenerational mobility (within a person's lifetime).

Education is the most important channel of upward mobility in modern society because it provides qualifications and skills for better jobs. Factors that limit mobility include poverty, caste discrimination, gender bias and unequal access to quality education.
Education is a social sub-system because it is one part of the larger social system and interacts with family, economy, politics and culture.

According to Talcott Parsons' structural-functional approach, society is a system made up of interrelated sub-systems (family, economy, polity, religion, education), each performing functions for the whole.

Education performs functions such as socialisation, transmission of culture, selection and allocation of people to roles, providing skilled manpower for the economy, and promoting social integration. Changes in other sub-systems (like technology or politics) bring changes in education, and vice versa.
Schools and colleges are social organisations with roles, rules, authority, relationships and common educational goals.

A school as a social organisation has a structure (head, teachers, students, staff), defined roles and status, rules and regulations, a common goal (education), and interactions among members. It also has an informal organisation of friendships and peer groups.

The school is called a 'miniature society' (Dewey) because it reflects the larger society. It connects with the community through parent-teacher associations, school management committees and community service. A democratic school climate promotes cooperation and good citizenship.
Social change means significant change in social relationships, institutions or patterns of life. Education can promote change by spreading knowledge, skills and new values.

Factors of social change include technology, economic changes, demographic changes, cultural contact, ideas and ideology, political movements and education. Change may be progressive or regressive, planned or unplanned.

Education acts both as a conservative force (preserving culture) and as a creative force (bringing change). It spreads scientific outlook, removes superstitions, empowers women and weaker sections, promotes democratic values and prepares people for new technologies.
Mass media can influence ideas, attitudes and behaviour and can spread information rapidly, making it an important means of social change.

Mass media include print media (newspapers, magazines, books), electronic media (radio, television, films) and new media (internet, social media, mobile apps). They inform, educate, entertain and shape public opinion.

In education, media are used for distance learning (Gyan Darshan, SWAYAM Prabha, DIKSHA), awareness campaigns and spreading new ideas. Negative effects include misinformation, violence, consumerism and addiction; hence media literacy is necessary.
Culture is the learned and shared way of life of a society, including beliefs, values, knowledge, customs, language and material objects.

E.B. Tylor defined culture as 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society'. Characteristics: culture is learned, shared, transmitted, symbolic, dynamic and varies from society to society.

Education preserves, transmits and enriches culture. Mizo culture, for example, includes values like 'tlawmngaihna' (selfless service), community festivals (Chapchar Kut, Mim Kut, Pawl Kut) and traditional dances like Cheraw, which can be promoted through education.
Material culture includes physical objects created by society, while non-material culture includes values, beliefs, norms, knowledge and customs.
Material culture includes tools, buildings, clothes, machines, technology and means of transport. Non-material culture includes language, beliefs, values, customs, laws, religion, art and literature.

Material culture changes quickly and is easy to borrow from other societies, while non-material culture changes slowly. Education transmits both, but its main focus is on non-material culture such as values, knowledge and attitudes.
Cultural lag occurs when material culture changes faster than non-material culture, creating a temporary gap in social adjustment.

The concept was introduced by William F. Ogburn in 1922. Example: mobile phones and the internet spread rapidly, but norms about their responsible use, privacy and cyber ethics develop more slowly. Similarly, modern medicine became available but superstitions about illness persisted.

Cultural lag can cause social problems and maladjustment. Education helps reduce cultural lag by spreading new knowledge, developing appropriate attitudes and values, and helping people adjust to technological change.
Education transmits culture from one generation to another but can also modify culture by introducing new knowledge, values and ways of thinking.

Functions of education in relation to culture: preservation (keeping traditions alive), transmission (passing culture to the next generation), modification (removing outdated customs like superstition and discrimination), enrichment (adding new knowledge) and integration (promoting unity in diversity).

The curriculum, co-curricular activities, celebration of festivals and teaching of mother tongue and local history help preserve culture, while science, critical thinking and contact with other cultures help bring cultural change.

Sociology studies society and social relationships, while education is an important social process. Educational Sociology examines how education is connected with social groups, culture and institutions.

A sociological approach is necessary because learners do not exist separately from society. Family background, community, peer groups, culture and social conditions influence educational experience.

Society consists of individuals, groups and institutions connected through social relationships. Education serves society by transmitting knowledge and culture, preparing individuals for social roles and contributing to social development.

Sociology and education: Sociology studies society, groups, institutions and social processes. Education is a social process and institution which socialises the young, transmits culture and prepares individuals for social roles.

Educational sociology: It studies the relationship between education and society - how social factors influence education and how education influences social life. It covers socialisation, social groups, stratification, mobility, social change and culture.

Need for sociological approach: Learners come from different social backgrounds of family, caste, class, religion and community, which affect their learning. A sociological approach helps teachers understand these influences, promote equality, prepare curriculum according to social needs and develop democratic citizenship.

Society: Society is a web of social relationships with shared norms and institutions. Education is both shaped by society and a means of improving society, which is why Dewey called the school a miniature society.

Socialization is the process by which an individual learns society's norms, values and expected behaviour. Family is the earliest agency, while school, community and peer group become increasingly important.

Primary groups involve close personal relationships, whereas secondary groups are more formal and goal-oriented. Both affect learning and social development.

Social control maintains accepted behaviour. Education contributes through discipline, values, rules and development of responsible citizenship.
Socialisation: It is the process of learning social norms, roles and values. Cooley's looking-glass self and Mead's theory of self explain how the self develops through interaction.

Agencies of socialisation: The family gives the first lessons in language, habits and values; the school provides formal learning, discipline and social skills; the community passes on customs and traditions; peer groups influence attitudes and behaviour; mass media and religion are also important.

Primary and secondary groups: Primary groups (family, friends) involve intimate, face-to-face relations and shape personality; secondary groups (associations, institutions) are formal and goal-oriented. Both influence learning and social development.

Social control: Society regulates behaviour by formal means (laws, rules) and informal means (customs, public opinion, religion). Education promotes social control by developing self-discipline, values and respect for law, while encouraging critical thinking.

Social stratification divides society into unequal positions or layers. Education can reflect existing inequality when access and opportunities differ, but it can also provide qualifications and opportunities that influence social position.

Social mobility means movement from one social position to another. Education is an important factor because knowledge and qualifications may improve occupational and social opportunities.

Education is itself a social sub-system, and educational institutions are social organisations connected with the wider social structure.

Social stratification: Stratification is the hierarchical arrangement of people based on caste, class, gender, wealth or power. In India, caste and class stratification have affected access to education.

Education and stratification: Education can reproduce inequality if quality education is limited to privileged groups, but it can also reduce inequality through free and compulsory education, scholarships, reservation and inclusive policies.

Social mobility: Mobility may be vertical or horizontal, intergenerational or intragenerational. Education is a major channel of upward mobility as it provides qualifications, skills and awareness needed for better jobs and status.
Conclusion: Education is a key instrument for creating an open, egalitarian society where status depends on merit and effort rather than birth, provided equal educational opportunities are ensured.

Social change is alteration in social relationships, institutions and ways of life. Education can act as an instrument of change by spreading knowledge and encouraging new attitudes. Mass media also contributes by rapidly communicating ideas and information.

Culture includes both material objects and non-material elements such as values and beliefs. Cultural lag occurs when different parts of culture change at unequal speeds.

Education preserves culture through transmission but also contributes to cultural change by encouraging critical thinking and introducing new knowledge.

Social change: Change in social structures, relationships and values occurs due to technology, economy, population, cultural contact and education. Education promotes change by spreading scientific outlook, removing superstitions, empowering weaker sections and preparing people for new roles.
Mass media: Media spread information quickly, influence attitudes and support distance education, but may also spread misinformation; media literacy is needed.
Culture: Culture is the learned and shared way of life, including material and non-material aspects. Education preserves, transmits, modifies and enriches culture.

Cultural lag: Ogburn's concept explains the gap between rapid material change and slower non-material change. Education helps bridge this gap by developing suitable values and attitudes, so that society adjusts smoothly to change.
Human rights are basic rights and freedoms belonging to every human being. They protect dignity, equality, liberty and security.

Characteristics of human rights: they are universal (belong to all people everywhere), inherent (by virtue of being human), inalienable (cannot be taken away), indivisible and interdependent (civil-political and economic-social rights are equally important).

Human rights include civil and political rights (right to life, liberty, equality, freedom of expression, fair trial, voting) and economic, social and cultural rights (right to work, education, health, social security and culture). Newer 'solidarity rights' include the right to development and a clean environment.
Ideas of rights developed over a long historical period and gained stronger international recognition after the Second World War.

Important milestones: Magna Carta (1215) in England limited royal power; the English Bill of Rights (1689); the American Declaration of Independence (1776); the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789); abolition of slavery in the 19th century.

After the horrors of World War II, the United Nations was formed in 1945, and its Charter promoted human rights. The UDHR (1948), the International Covenants (1966) and later conventions created an international human rights system.
The UDHR was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948 and sets out a broad international statement of fundamental human rights and freedoms.
The UDHR was adopted on 10 December 1948 in Paris; this date is celebrated as Human Rights Day. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. It has a preamble and 30 articles.

Articles 1-2 state equality and non-discrimination; Articles 3-21 cover civil and political rights (life, liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, equality before law, freedom of thought, expression and assembly); Articles 22-27 cover economic, social and cultural rights (social security, work, education, rest, standard of living, culture); Articles 28-30 speak of social order and duties. Along with the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) it forms the International Bill of Human Rights.
The Constitution protects important human rights through Fundamental Rights and other constitutional provisions based on justice, liberty, equality and dignity.

Part III (Articles 12-35) guarantees Fundamental Rights: right to equality (14-18), right to freedom (19-22), right against exploitation (23-24), right to freedom of religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30) and right to constitutional remedies (32). Article 21A (added by the 86th Amendment, 2002) gives the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

Part IV, the Directive Principles of State Policy, includes economic and social rights such as right to work, living wage and public assistance. Part IVA lists Fundamental Duties. The Supreme Court has expanded Article 21 to include the right to livelihood, privacy, health and a clean environment.
The NHRC is an institution for the protection and promotion of human rights in India under the relevant legal framework.

The NHRC was established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It consists of a Chairperson (a former Chief Justice of India or judge of the Supreme Court) and members, along with ex-officio members from other national commissions.

Functions: inquiring into complaints of human rights violations, intervening in court cases, visiting jails and institutions, reviewing laws, promoting research and spreading human rights literacy. Its recommendations are advisory. States have State Human Rights Commissions; the Mizoram State Human Rights Commission was set up in 2005.
Human Rights Education teaches knowledge, values and attitudes needed to understand, respect and protect human rights.

The UN declared 1995-2004 the United Nations Decade for Human Rights Education, and the World Programme for Human Rights Education began in 2005. Human rights education includes education about rights (knowledge), through rights (respectful learning environment) and for rights (empowering people to exercise and defend rights).
It can be imparted through the curriculum, co-curricular activities, observance of Human Rights Day, debates, role plays and community activities.
Its aims include awareness of rights and duties, respect for dignity and equality, prevention of discrimination and development of responsible citizenship.

Specific aims: (1) to provide knowledge of human rights documents and constitutional provisions; (2) to develop respect for human dignity and diversity; (3) to promote gender equality and tolerance; (4) to develop skills to protect rights and seek remedies; (5) to promote democratic participation and responsible citizenship; (6) to build a culture of peace and non-violence.
It also aims to make people aware of duties along with rights, as rights and duties go together.
Human Rights Education helps individuals recognise violations, respect the rights of others and build a democratic and peaceful society.

Need: human rights violations such as discrimination based on caste, gender and religion, child labour, trafficking, custodial violence and violence against women still occur. Many people are unaware of their rights and remedies.

Importance: it empowers individuals, protects vulnerable groups, strengthens democracy and the rule of law, promotes peace, tolerance and national integration, and helps achieve the goals of the Constitution such as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
Important principles include equality, dignity, non-discrimination, participation, respect and responsibility.

Principles: universality and inalienability; indivisibility and interdependence of rights; equality and non-discrimination; participation and inclusion; accountability and rule of law; learner-centred and participatory methods.

The teaching methods should be democratic and experiential - discussions, case studies, role plays, projects and field visits - so that learners both understand and practise human rights in daily life.
Children have rights to survival, protection, development, education and participation appropriate to their age and circumstances.

The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) was adopted in 1989 and ratified by India in 1992. It defines a child as a person below 18 years and groups rights into survival, development, protection and participation rights.

Indian laws include Article 21A and the RTE Act 2009, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 (amended 2016), the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015, the POCSO Act 2012 and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) was set up in 2007.
Women's human rights include equality, dignity, freedom from discrimination and violence and equal opportunity.
The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW, 1979) is known as the international bill of rights for women; India ratified it in 1993.

Constitutional provisions include Articles 14, 15(3), 16 and 39, and reservation in panchayats and municipalities (73rd and 74th Amendments). Laws include the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 and the Women's Reservation Act 2023. The National Commission for Women was set up in 1992.
Minority rights protect equality, identity, culture and freedom from discrimination.

The UN Declaration on the Rights of Persons Belonging to National or Ethnic, Religious and Linguistic Minorities was adopted in 1992. In India, Articles 29 and 30 protect the right of minorities to conserve their language, script and culture and to establish and administer educational institutions.

The National Commission for Minorities Act 1992 created the National Commission for Minorities. Six communities - Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains - are notified as national minorities. Mizoram has a Christian majority, while Christians are a minority at the national level.
Persons with disabilities are entitled to dignity, equality, accessibility, participation and protection from discrimination.
The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) was adopted in 2006, and India ratified it in 2007. It emphasises accessibility, inclusion, equality and non-discrimination.

In India, the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognises 21 types of disabilities, provides 4 per cent reservation in government jobs and 5 per cent in higher education, and promotes inclusive education. The Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) aims to make public places and transport accessible.

Human rights are basic rights and freedoms necessary for human dignity. Their modern international development was strongly shaped by the experience of war and the need for common standards.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, states fundamental civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. In India, constitutional provisions, especially Fundamental Rights, protect important aspects of liberty and equality.

The National Human Rights Commission contributes to the protection and promotion of human rights within India's legal framework.

Meaning and characteristics: Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of nationality, sex, caste, religion or any other status. They are universal, inalienable, indivisible and interdependent, and include civil-political as well as economic-social-cultural rights.

Historical development: The ideas of rights grew through Magna Carta (1215), the English Bill of Rights (1689), the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the French Declaration (1789). After World War II, the United Nations made human rights a central principle.

UDHR: Adopted on 10 December 1948, the UDHR's 30 articles cover equality, life, liberty, freedom from torture and slavery, fair trial, freedom of expression and religion, right to education, work and social security. With the two Covenants of 1966, it forms the International Bill of Human Rights.

Indian Constitution and NHRC: Fundamental Rights (Part III), Directive Principles (Part IV) and Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) protect human rights in India. The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 established the NHRC and State Human Rights Commissions to inquire into violations, spread awareness and advise the government.

Human Rights Education develops knowledge of rights and responsibilities together with attitudes of equality, dignity and respect. Its aim is not only to teach legal provisions but also to develop behaviour that respects the rights of others.

It is important for preventing discrimination, increasing awareness and strengthening democratic citizenship. Its principles include dignity, equality, non-discrimination, participation and responsibility.
Meaning: Human Rights Education is education about, through and for human rights. It provides knowledge, develops attitudes of respect and equality, and builds skills to defend rights.
Aims: awareness of rights and duties, respect for dignity and diversity, gender equality, elimination of prejudice, active democratic citizenship and promotion of peace.

Need and importance: Violations of rights still occur, and many people are unaware of their rights. HRE empowers individuals, protects vulnerable groups, strengthens democracy and promotes social justice.

Principles and methods: HRE follows universality, equality, non-discrimination, participation and accountability. It is best taught through participatory methods - discussions, debates, role plays, case studies, projects and celebration of days like Human Rights Day - and by creating a school environment where rights are respected.

Children require special protection because of their age and dependence and have rights connected with survival, development, protection and education. Women have equal human rights and require protection from discrimination and violence.

Minorities possess rights to equality and protection of identity and culture, while persons with disabilities are entitled to dignity, accessibility, participation and non-discrimination.

Human Rights Education helps learners understand these rights and develop respect for diversity.

Rights of children: The UNCRC (1989) recognises survival, development, protection and participation rights. Indian laws such as the RTE Act 2009, POCSO Act 2012, Juvenile Justice Act 2015 and the Child Labour Act protect children, and the NCPCR monitors child rights.

Rights of women: CEDAW (1979) and constitutional provisions promote equality. Laws against dowry, domestic violence and sexual harassment, and bodies like the National Commission for Women protect women's rights.
Rights of minorities: Articles 29 and 30 protect minorities' cultural and educational rights, and the National Commission for Minorities safeguards their interests.

Rights of persons with disabilities: The UNCRPD (2006) and the RPWD Act 2016 ensure equality, accessibility, inclusive education and reservation. Education plays an important role in spreading awareness and building an inclusive society that respects the rights of all vulnerable groups.
Philosophy is the systematic study of fundamental questions about reality, knowledge and values. Its major branches in the syllabus are metaphysics, epistemology and axiology.
The word philosophy comes from the Greek words 'philos' (love) and 'sophia' (wisdom), meaning love of wisdom. In India it is called 'darshana', meaning vision of truth.

Its three main branches are metaphysics (reality), epistemology (knowledge) and axiology (values, including ethics and aesthetics). Logic, which studies correct reasoning, is sometimes added as a fourth branch. Philosophy helps answer basic questions about the purpose of life and education.
Metaphysics studies the nature of reality and existence.

Metaphysics deals with questions such as: What is real - matter or mind? What is the nature of the self, the soul and God? Is the universe created or eternal? Branches include ontology (nature of being), cosmology (origin of the universe) and theology.

In education, metaphysical beliefs determine the aims of education. For example, idealists who believe that ultimate reality is spiritual stress spiritual development, while naturalists who believe reality is matter emphasise natural growth.
Epistemology studies knowledge, including its nature, possibility and sources.

Epistemology asks: What is knowledge? How do we know? What are the sources and limits of knowledge? Sources include sense experience (empiricism), reason (rationalism), intuition, authority and revelation. Indian philosophy recognises pramanas such as perception (pratyaksha), inference (anumana) and verbal testimony (shabda).
Epistemology helps in deciding the curriculum and methods of teaching, for example whether learning should be through experience and experiment or through reasoning and texts.
Axiology studies values and includes questions of what is good, right and beautiful.

Axiology has two branches: ethics (moral values - good and bad, right and wrong) and aesthetics (beauty and art). Values may be intrinsic (valuable in themselves, like truth) or instrumental (valuable as means, like money).
In education, axiology guides the selection of values to be taught, such as truth, honesty, non-violence, cooperation and appreciation of beauty, and influences moral education and discipline.
Philosophy provides aims, values and ideas about knowledge and human life, while education puts many of these ideas into practice.

Philosophy and education are closely related: philosophy is the theory and education is the practice. John Adams said, 'Education is the dynamic side of philosophy.' Gentile said that education without philosophy would be blind and philosophy without education would be crippled.

Philosophy determines the aims of education, curriculum, methods of teaching, role of the teacher, discipline, textbooks and evaluation. Great philosophers like Plato, Rousseau, Dewey, Gandhi and Tagore were also great educators.
Educational philosophy studies philosophical questions relating to aims, curriculum, teaching, discipline, knowledge and the role of teachers.

Educational philosophy is the application of philosophical principles to education. It answers questions like: What should be the aims of education? What should be taught? How should it be taught? What should be the relationship between teacher and pupil?

Its functions include speculative (developing theories), normative (setting standards and aims), analytical (clarifying concepts) and critical (evaluating educational practices). It guides teachers in making thoughtful decisions.
Knowledge means justified understanding or awareness. Sources may include experience, reason, observation and other recognised means of knowing.

Types of knowledge include a priori knowledge (independent of experience, e.g. mathematics), a posteriori knowledge (based on experience), propositional knowledge (knowing that), procedural knowledge (knowing how) and tacit knowledge.

Sources: senses, reason, intuition, authority (teachers, books, experts), testimony and revelation. Education should help students use multiple sources of knowledge critically, verify information and construct knowledge actively.
Idealism gives primary importance to mind, ideas and spiritual values. In education it emphasizes character, values, intellectual development and the teacher's important role.

Main exponents: Plato, Hegel, Kant, Froebel, Swami Vivekananda, Mahatma Gandhi and Tagore. Idealism holds that ideas and mind are the ultimate reality and that eternal values of truth, beauty and goodness (satyam, shivam, sundaram) are supreme.

Aims of education: self-realisation, spiritual and moral development, character building and development of personality. Curriculum: humanities, religion, ethics, literature, history and fine arts. Methods: lecture, discussion, questioning (Socratic method) and imitation. The teacher is highly respected as a friend, philosopher and guide.
Realism emphasizes an objective world independent of the individual mind. Education should provide knowledge of reality through observation, experience and systematic study.
Exponents include Aristotle, John Locke, Comenius, Herbart and Bertrand Russell. Realism has forms such as humanistic realism, social realism and sense realism.

Aims of education: preparing the child for real life, developing physical and mental powers, vocational efficiency and knowledge of the natural and social world. Curriculum: science, mathematics, vocational subjects and languages. Methods: observation, experiment, demonstration, field trips and the use of audio-visual aids. Realism encouraged the scientific and objective approach in education.
Naturalism emphasizes nature and the natural development of the child. Education should allow freedom and learning through direct experience.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, author of 'Emile' (1762), is the chief exponent; others include Herbert Spencer, Tagore and Bernard Shaw. Rousseau said, 'Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature; everything degenerates in the hands of man.'

Aims: natural development of the child, self-preservation and happiness. Curriculum: nature study, physical activities, games and practical subjects. Methods: learning by doing, play-way method, observation and heuristic method. The teacher is a stage-setter and observer; discipline comes through natural consequences. Negative education in early years was emphasised.
Pragmatism emphasizes experience, action and practical consequences. Education is learner-centred and often uses activity, problem-solving and learning by doing.

Exponents include Charles Peirce, William James and John Dewey. Pragmatism holds that truth is what works in practice and that values are changing and relative. Dewey's slogan was 'learning by doing'.

Aims: social efficiency, development of a democratic citizen, problem-solving ability and continuous growth. Curriculum: integrated, activity-centred and related to life (utility, interest, experience). Methods: project method (Kilpatrick), problem-solving method and experiential learning. The teacher is a guide and helper; discipline is social and self-imposed through group activities.
Sankhya explains reality through Purusha and Prakriti. Its educational implications include self-knowledge, disciplined development and understanding of the individual.

Sankhya, founded by Sage Kapila, is a dualistic philosophy. Purusha is pure consciousness and Prakriti is matter, made up of three gunas - sattva (purity), rajas (activity) and tamas (inertia). Bondage results from ignorance of the distinction between Purusha and Prakriti, and liberation (kaivalya) comes through discriminative knowledge.

Educational implications: the aim is self-realisation and liberation; education should develop the body, senses and mind in a balanced way; curriculum should include natural sciences, ethics, yoga and philosophy; methods include reasoning, discussion, meditation and practical experience; the teacher is a guide who helps the student discriminate between the real and unreal.
Vedanta emphasizes ultimate reality and self-realisation. Education is connected with knowledge, moral development and realization of the higher self.

Vedanta, based on the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and the Bhagavad Gita, teaches that Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (self) are one. Shankaracharya's Advaita Vedanta says the world is maya (appearance) and liberation comes through knowledge (jnana).

Educational implications: the aim is self-realisation and moral and spiritual development; the curriculum includes spiritual texts, ethics and sciences; methods include shravana (listening), manana (reflection) and nididhyasana (meditation); the guru-shishya relationship is central; discipline is self-control. Swami Vivekananda applied Vedanta to modern education: 'Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.'
Buddhist thought emphasizes suffering, right conduct, wisdom and disciplined living. Its educational implications include moral development, self-discipline and understanding.

Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha in the 6th century BC. Its teachings include the Four Noble Truths (suffering, cause of suffering, end of suffering, path to end suffering) and the Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration).

Educational implications: the aim is the all-round development of personality and attainment of nirvana; education was open to all irrespective of caste; monasteries (viharas) and universities like Nalanda, Taxila and Vikramshila became great centres of learning; methods included discussion, debate, lectures and meditation; the medium of instruction was the language of the people (Pali).
Jainism emphasizes non-violence, self-control and right knowledge. Education should promote moral discipline, tolerance and responsible conduct.

Jainism was propagated by Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara. Its central teachings are the three jewels (triratna) - right faith, right knowledge and right conduct - and five vows: non-violence (ahimsa), truth (satya), non-stealing (asteya), celibacy (brahmacharya) and non-possession (aparigraha). Anekantavada teaches that truth has many aspects.

Educational implications: aims include character building, self-discipline and liberation; the curriculum includes ethics, philosophy and practical skills; methods include lectures, discussions and self-study; the teacher should be of high moral character. Anekantavada encourages tolerance and respect for different viewpoints.
Krishnamurti emphasized freedom from fear and conditioning, self-knowledge and education for the development of the whole human being.

Jiddu Krishnamurti (1895-1986) believed that education should free the mind from fear, conditioning, competition and authority. He founded schools such as Rishi Valley (Andhra Pradesh) and Brockwood Park (England).

Aims: understanding oneself, development of the whole person (intellectual, emotional and spiritual), creative intelligence and goodness. He opposed rote learning, comparison and examinations-based fear. The teacher should be a friend who learns along with the student; a free and affectionate environment is needed for true learning.
Radhakrishnan emphasized spiritual and moral development, knowledge and the role of education in developing the whole person.

Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (1888-1975) was a philosopher, teacher and the second President of India; his birthday, 5 September, is celebrated as Teachers' Day. He chaired the University Education Commission (1948-49).

He believed that education should develop the whole man - physical, intellectual, moral and spiritual. Aims: character building, search for truth, democratic citizenship and national integration. He recommended religious and moral education (not dogmatic), rural universities, emphasis on general education and the use of the mother tongue. Teachers should be scholars and models of character.
Kant gave importance to reason, morality and human autonomy. Education contributes to disciplined freedom and moral development.

Immanuel Kant (1724-1804), a German philosopher, wrote 'On Education' (lectures, published 1803). He said, 'Man can only become man by education.' He gave importance to the categorical imperative: act only according to the rule that you would want to become a universal law.

Educational ideas: education has stages of discipline (taming), culture (instruction), civilisation (social manners) and moralisation (moral character). Aims include autonomy, moral character, reason and freedom with responsibility. He favoured both physical and practical education and believed in treating each person as an end, not a means.
Marx connected education with society, labour and class relations. His thought encourages examination of how social and economic structures influence education.

Karl Marx (1818-1883) believed that education is shaped by the economic structure of society and serves the interests of the ruling class in capitalism. He advocated polytechnical education, which combines intellectual education, physical education and productive labour.

Educational implications: free public education for all children, abolition of child labour in factories, combination of education with productive work, development of all-round personality and class consciousness. Marxist ideas influenced socialist education systems and critical pedagogy (Paulo Freire).

Philosophy studies fundamental questions concerning reality, knowledge and values. Metaphysics studies reality, epistemology studies knowledge and axiology studies values.

Education is closely related to philosophy because educational aims, curriculum, methods and discipline depend on beliefs about the learner, knowledge and society. Educational philosophy applies philosophical thinking to educational problems.

Knowledge may arise from experience, reason and other recognised sources. The philosophical foundation of education therefore helps teachers understand why education follows particular aims and methods.
Meaning of philosophy: Philosophy is the love of wisdom and a systematic inquiry into the nature of reality, knowledge and values. Its main branches are metaphysics, epistemology and axiology.

Relationship between philosophy and education: Philosophy and education are two sides of the same coin. Philosophy gives the goals and values; education provides the means to realise them. Philosophy determines aims, curriculum, methods, teacher's role, discipline and evaluation.

Educational philosophy: It applies philosophical thinking to educational problems and performs speculative, normative, analytical and critical functions. It helps teachers examine their beliefs and practices.

Knowledge and its sources: Knowledge may be gained through senses, reason, intuition, authority and revelation. Different philosophies emphasise different sources: idealists stress reason and intuition, realists and pragmatists stress experience and experiment. Understanding these helps teachers choose appropriate methods.

Idealism emphasizes mind, ideas and spiritual values and gives importance to moral and intellectual development. Realism emphasizes the objective world and knowledge gained through systematic observation and experience.

Naturalism gives priority to nature and the child's natural development, supporting freedom and direct experience. Pragmatism views knowledge in relation to experience and practical action and emphasizes problem-solving and learning by doing.

Each school influences educational aims, curriculum, teaching methods, discipline and the role of the teacher in different ways.

Idealism: Reality is spiritual and mental; values are absolute. Aims are self-realisation, moral and spiritual development and character. The curriculum emphasises humanities, religion and ethics; methods include lecture, discussion and questioning; the teacher is central and highly respected.

Realism: The external world is real and independent of the mind. Aims are preparation for life and knowledge of reality. The curriculum stresses science and practical subjects; methods include observation, experiment and audio-visual aids.

Naturalism: Nature is the ultimate reality; the child should grow naturally. Rousseau's 'Emile' advocated freedom, learning from nature, play-way methods, negative education in early years and discipline by natural consequences. The child is the centre of education.

Pragmatism: Truth is what works; values change. Dewey emphasised experience, problem-solving, democracy and social efficiency. The curriculum is activity-centred and integrated; the project method is widely used. Modern education combines the strengths of these philosophies - values from idealism, science from realism, child-centredness from naturalism and activity from pragmatism.

Sankhya explains reality through Purusha and Prakriti and has implications for disciplined self-development. Vedanta emphasizes ultimate reality and self-realisation and connects education with moral and spiritual growth.

Buddhism stresses right conduct, wisdom and disciplined living, while Jainism emphasizes non-violence, self-control and right knowledge.

These schools show that Indian philosophical traditions connect education with development of knowledge, character and the self.

Sankhya: A dualistic system explaining reality through Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter with three gunas). Education aims at discriminative knowledge and liberation, with balanced development of body, mind and senses.

Vedanta: Teaches the unity of Atman and Brahman. Education aims at self-realisation and moral and spiritual growth through shravana, manana and nididhyasana under a guru. Vivekananda described education as the manifestation of perfection already in man.

Buddhism: Based on the Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path, Buddhist education was open to all, used the people's language, and developed great universities like Nalanda and Taxila. It emphasised moral conduct, meditation and wisdom.

Jainism: Based on right faith, right knowledge and right conduct and the vow of non-violence, Jain education aims at character and self-discipline. Its doctrine of anekantavada teaches tolerance. Indian philosophies emphasise the moral and spiritual dimension of education, which remains relevant in value education today.

sections.title: Educational Thought of Krishnamurti, Radhakrishnan, Kant and Marx

blocks.text:
Jiddu Krishnamurti emphasized freedom from fear and conditioning, self-understanding and development of the whole person. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan emphasized moral and spiritual development along with knowledge.

Immanuel Kant gave importance to reason, autonomy and moral discipline. Karl Marx connected education with labour, society and class relations and drew attention to the social and economic context of education.

Their educational ideas differ, but all raise important questions about the purpose of education and the kind of person and society education should help create.

Jiddu Krishnamurti: Education should free the mind from fear, conditioning and competition and help students understand themselves. He opposed authority, comparison and examinations-based learning and emphasised the whole development of the child in schools like Rishi Valley.

Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan: As chairman of the University Education Commission, he emphasised moral and spiritual values, character, democratic citizenship and the search for truth. He saw teachers as the builders of the nation.
Immanuel Kant: Kant stressed reason, moral duty and autonomy. Education passes through discipline, culture, civilisation and moralisation, aiming to make man truly human and morally free.

Karl Marx: Marx viewed education as linked to the economic structure and class relations. He advocated free public education combined with productive labour (polytechnical education) to develop all-round individuals. These thinkers show different perspectives - spiritual, moral, rational and social - which together enrich educational thought.

sections.title: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION
SHORT NOTES
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

sections.title: Universalization of Elementary Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Universalization of Elementary Education seeks to ensure access, enrolment, participation and completion of elementary education for all children.

UEE has three components: universal access (a school within reach of every child), universal enrolment (all children aged 6-14 enrolled), universal retention (children stay and complete the stage) and universal achievement (minimum levels of learning). Article 45 originally directed the state to provide free and compulsory education, and Article 21A (2002) made it a fundamental right.

Major programmes include Operation Blackboard (1987), DPEP (1994), Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001), Mid-Day Meal (now PM POSHAN), the RTE Act 2009 and Samagra Shiksha (2018). Challenges include dropout, poor learning outcomes (shown by ASER and NAS surveys), teacher shortages and inclusion of disadvantaged groups.

sections.title: NCERT
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The National Council of Educational Research and Training supports school education through research, curriculum development, textbooks, training and academic assistance.

NCERT was established in 1961 as an autonomous organisation under the Ministry of Education, with headquarters in New Delhi. Its constituent units include the National Institute of Education, CIET, PSSCIVE (Bhopal) and Regional Institutes of Education (including the North-East RIE at Shillong).

Functions: developing the National Curriculum Framework (NCF 2005, NCF-SE 2023), preparing textbooks, conducting research and surveys such as the National Achievement Survey, training teachers, and organising the National Talent Search. It advises the government on school education policies.

sections.title: DIET
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: District Institutes of Education and Training provide teacher education, training and academic support mainly at the elementary level.
DIETs were established following the National Policy on Education 1986 under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Teacher Education. Each district is to have a DIET.

Functions: pre-service training (D.El.Ed.), in-service training of elementary teachers, action research, development of local teaching materials, academic support to Block and Cluster Resource Centres, and planning and management of elementary education at the district level. Mizoram has DIETs in its districts supported by the SCERT.

sections.title: Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Samagra Shiksha is an integrated school-education programme intended to support access, equity and quality across school education.

Samagra Shiksha was launched in 2018 by merging Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and Teacher Education. It covers school education from pre-school to class XII as a continuum.

Its objectives include universal access, quality education, equity and inclusion, gender equality, vocational education, digital education, support for children with special needs and strengthening of teacher education institutions. It has been aligned with NEP 2020 and includes initiatives such as NIPUN Bharat for foundational literacy and numeracy.

sections.title: Problems of Secondary Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Secondary education faces issues such as access, dropout, quality, infrastructure, teacher availability, examination pressure and relevance of curriculum.

Problems: (1) inadequate access, especially in rural and hilly areas; (2) high dropout rates, particularly among girls and disadvantaged groups; (3) shortage of qualified teachers in science and mathematics; (4) poor infrastructure such as laboratories and libraries; (5) examination-oriented rote learning; (6) lack of vocational education; (7) inadequate guidance and counselling.

Remedies: expanding schools, scholarships, teacher recruitment and training, ICT and smart classes, vocational education, examination reform, guidance services and community participation. The Kothari Commission (1964-66) and NEP 2020 recommended many of these reforms.

sections.title: NUEPA
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The National University of Educational Planning and Administration, as named in the syllabus, is associated with educational planning, administration, training and research.

NUEPA originated as the Asian Regional Centre for Educational Planners and Administrators (1962), became the National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration (NIEPA) in 1979, and became NUEPA, a deemed university, in 2006. It is now called the National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration (NIEPA) again.

Functions: training of educational planners and administrators, research in educational planning and policy, consultancy to central and state governments, and managing data systems such as the earlier DISE (now UDISE+, managed by the Ministry of Education).

sections.title: CBSE
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The Central Board of Secondary Education is a national-level school education board responsible for functions such as affiliation, curriculum-related work and examinations within its system.
CBSE was established in 1929 and reconstituted in 1962; its headquarters is in New Delhi. It affiliates schools across India and abroad, including Kendriya Vidyalayas and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas.

Functions: conducting Class X and XII examinations, prescribing syllabus mainly based on NCERT textbooks, granting affiliation, training teachers, and promoting innovations such as competency-based education.
