It earlier conducted entrance examinations like NEET and JEE, which are now conducted by the National Testing Agency.

sections.title: MBSE
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The Mizoram Board of School Education performs school-board functions in Mizoram, including academic and examination responsibilities under its mandate.
The MBSE was established in 1975 under the Mizoram Board of School Education Act and has its headquarters in Aizawl.

Functions: prescribing curriculum and syllabus for classes in Mizoram schools, preparing and approving textbooks, conducting the HSLC (Class X) and HSSLC (Class XII) examinations, granting recognition to schools, publishing results and promoting the use of Mizo language and culture in education.

sections.title: Population Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Population Education develops understanding of population issues and their relationship with quality of life, resources and development.

Population education was introduced in India in 1969 under a national programme supported by UNFPA. It is not the same as family planning; it focuses on understanding population dynamics and their impact on quality of life.

Content: population growth and its causes, effects on resources, environment, health, education and employment, family size and welfare, gender equality and adolescent health. Methods include integration into existing subjects, discussions, projects and surveys.

sections.title: Sex Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Sex Education provides age-appropriate knowledge about human sexuality, health, relationships and responsible behaviour.

Sex education includes knowledge of human reproduction, puberty and physical changes, personal hygiene, responsible relationships, prevention of sexual abuse, HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infections, and gender equality.

It helps adolescents make informed and responsible decisions, protects them from exploitation and misinformation, and promotes healthy attitudes. In India, it is provided through the Adolescence Education Programme (AEP) and School Health Programme under Ayushman Bharat. It should be culturally sensitive and taught by trained teachers.

sections.title: Environmental Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Environmental Education develops awareness, knowledge, attitudes and responsible action for environmental protection.

The Tbilisi Declaration (1977) set the objectives of environmental education: awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation. In India, the Supreme Court (M.C. Mehta case, 1991) directed that environmental education be made compulsory at all levels.

Methods include field trips, nature clubs (eco-clubs under the National Green Corps), projects, celebration of environment days, tree plantation and cleanliness drives. It helps students understand problems like pollution, deforestation and climate change and adopt sustainable lifestyles.

sections.title: Value Oriented Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: Value Oriented Education promotes moral, social and human values through educational experiences.

Values include personal values (honesty, self-discipline), social values (cooperation, respect, tolerance), national values (patriotism, democracy, secularism) and universal values (truth, non-violence, love, peace). The Constitution's Preamble provides values such as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

Value education can be imparted through the curriculum, morning assemblies, stories, role models, co-curricular activities, community service and the example of teachers. Commissions such as the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020 emphasised value-based education.

sections.title: Right to Education Act, 2009
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 provides the legal framework for free and compulsory elementary education for children in the prescribed age group.

The RTE Act came into force on 1 April 2010. It gives every child aged 6-14 the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until completion of elementary education (Classes I-VIII).

Key provisions: 25 per cent reservation for disadvantaged children in private unaided schools; norms for pupil-teacher ratio (30:1 at primary, 35:1 at upper primary), buildings and teachers; prohibition of capitation fees, screening, physical punishment and mental harassment; School Management Committees with parents; trained teachers; and Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation. The 2019 amendment allowed states to hold back students failing in Classes V and VIII.

sections.title: E-learning
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: E-learning uses digital and electronic technologies to support teaching and learning.

Forms of e-learning include online courses, virtual classrooms, video lectures, e-books, educational apps, learning management systems and MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses). It may be synchronous (live) or asynchronous (self-paced).

Indian initiatives include SWAYAM, SWAYAM Prabha DTH channels, DIKSHA, e-Pathshala, National Digital Library and PM e-VIDYA. Advantages: flexibility, access to quality content, self-paced learning. Challenges: digital divide, lack of devices and internet in rural and hilly areas like Mizoram, and less personal interaction.

sections.title: Vocational Education under NEP 2020
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: The syllabus highlights vocational education as an initiative under NEP 2020, linking education more closely with skills and work experience.

NEP 2020 aims to integrate vocational education with mainstream education so that at least 50 per cent of learners get exposure to vocational education by 2025. Students in Classes 6-8 will do a 10-day bagless period with local vocational experts such as carpenters, gardeners and potters.

It proposes removing hard separation between academic and vocational streams, aligning courses with the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF), offering vocational courses in higher education and collaboration with industry and ITIs. This will improve employability and dignity of labour.

sections.title: School Structure under NEP 2020
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: NEP 2020 proposes a 5+3+3+4 curricular and pedagogical structure for school education.

The 5+3+3+4 structure replaces the earlier 10+2 system: (1) Foundational Stage - 5 years (3 years of pre-school/Anganwadi and Classes 1-2, ages 3-8); (2) Preparatory Stage - 3 years (Classes 3-5, ages 8-11); (3) Middle Stage - 3 years (Classes 6-8, ages 11-14); (4) Secondary Stage - 4 years (Classes 9-12, ages 14-18).

It emphasises early childhood care and education, foundational literacy and numeracy, play-based and activity-based learning, experiential learning, flexibility in subject choices, and board examinations that test core competencies rather than rote memory.

sections.title: Higher Education under NEP 2020
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text: NEP 2020 proposes multidisciplinary and flexible higher education with reforms in curriculum, institutions and undergraduate education.

Main proposals: increasing the Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education to 50 per cent by 2035; multidisciplinary universities and colleges; a four-year undergraduate programme with multiple entry and exit options (certificate after 1 year, diploma after 2 years, degree after 3 years, honours or research degree after 4 years); Academic Bank of Credits.

It also proposes a single regulator, the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI), a National Research Foundation, the Common University Entrance Test (CUET), internationalisation and greater use of online education. Colleges are to become autonomous degree-granting institutions over time.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

sections.title: Elementary Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Universalization of Elementary Education aims to ensure that all children can enter, participate in and complete elementary schooling. Access alone is not enough; equity and quality are also necessary.

NCERT provides academic support through curriculum, research, textbooks and training. DIETs support teacher education and academic development at the district level. Samagra Shiksha integrates support for school education and seeks improvements in access, equity and quality.

These institutions and programmes form important parts of contemporary school education in India.

UEE: Universalisation of elementary education means ensuring access, enrolment, retention and achievement for all children aged 6-14. Article 21A and the RTE Act 2009 made it a fundamental right. Programmes like Operation Blackboard, DPEP, SSA, Mid-Day Meal and Samagra Shiksha have increased enrolment, but learning quality and dropout remain challenges.

NCERT: Established in 1961, NCERT develops curriculum frameworks and textbooks, conducts research and surveys, and trains teachers. It plays a central role in improving the quality of school education.
DIET: DIETs provide pre-service and in-service teacher training, develop local materials, conduct action research and give academic support to schools at the district level.

Samagra Shiksha: This integrated scheme (2018) treats school education from pre-school to Class XII as a continuum, focusing on access, equity, quality, inclusion, vocational and digital education. Together these institutions and programmes work to achieve quality elementary education for all.

sections.title: Secondary Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Secondary education faces problems including unequal access, dropout, inadequate infrastructure, teacher shortages, examination pressure and questions about curriculum relevance. Solutions require better facilities, trained teachers, academic support and stronger planning.

The syllabus identifies NUEPA for educational planning and administration, CBSE as a national school board and MBSE as the school education board in Mizoram. These organisations perform different planning, academic and examination-related functions.

Problems of secondary education: lack of access in remote areas, high dropout, poor infrastructure, shortage of subject teachers, outdated curriculum, examination pressure and rote learning, lack of vocational options and guidance.
Remedies: expansion of schools, scholarships, teacher training, ICT-enabled learning, vocationalisation, examination reform, guidance and counselling.

Institutions: NUEPA/NIEPA trains educational planners and administrators and conducts research on policy; CBSE conducts examinations and affiliates schools across India; MBSE prescribes curriculum, prepares textbooks and conducts HSLC and HSSLC examinations in Mizoram.
Conclusion: Improving secondary education requires coordinated efforts by national and state bodies, adequate funding and reforms recommended by commissions like the Kothari Commission and NEP 2020.

sections.title: Population, Sex, Environmental and Value Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text:
Population Education helps learners understand population and its relationship with resources and development. Sex Education provides responsible and age-appropriate understanding of sexuality, health and relationships.

Environmental Education develops awareness and responsible behaviour toward the environment. Value Oriented Education promotes moral and social values.

These areas are important because contemporary education must prepare learners not only academically but also for responsible personal and social life.

Population education: It helps learners understand population growth and its effects on quality of life, resources and development, and promotes responsible attitudes toward family size and gender equality.
Sex education: Age-appropriate knowledge of puberty, reproduction, hygiene, relationships, prevention of abuse and HIV/AIDS helps adolescents make responsible choices and stay safe.

Environmental education: Following the Tbilisi principles, it develops awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation for protecting the environment. Eco-clubs, projects and field trips are effective methods.

Value-oriented education: It develops personal, social, national and universal values such as honesty, respect, cooperation, secularism and peace. These areas of education together help create responsible, healthy and caring citizens.

sections.title: Modern Trends in Indian Education
context: EDU 104 – ISSUES AND TRENDS IN CONTEMPORARY INDIAN EDUCATION

blocks.text:
The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives a legal framework to free and compulsory elementary education for children in the prescribed age group. E-learning uses digital technology to support learning and has become an important modern educational method.

NEP 2020 gives importance to vocational education and proposes a 5+3+3+4 structure for school education. In higher education, it emphasizes flexibility, multidisciplinary learning and institutional reform.

These developments show the changing structure and priorities of contemporary Indian education.

RTE Act 2009: It guarantees free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14, reserves 25 per cent seats in private schools for disadvantaged children, sets norms for schools and teachers, prohibits corporal punishment and screening, and establishes School Management Committees.
E-learning: Digital platforms like SWAYAM, DIKSHA and SWAYAM Prabha offer flexible learning. E-learning gained importance during the COVID-19 pandemic but faces challenges of the digital divide.

NEP 2020 in school education: The 5+3+3+4 structure, focus on foundational literacy and numeracy, mother tongue as medium up to at least Class 5 where possible, vocational exposure from Class 6, and competency-based assessment.

NEP 2020 in higher education: Multidisciplinary institutions, four-year undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit, Academic Bank of Credits, a single regulator (HECI), research funding and a target GER of 50 per cent by 2035. These trends aim to make Indian education more inclusive, flexible and skill-oriented.
Peace is more than absence of war. It includes conditions of security, justice, cooperation and healthy human relationships.

The word 'peace' comes from the Latin 'pax'. In Indian thought, 'shanti' refers to inner peace and harmony with others and nature. Peace has different levels: inner peace (within the individual), social peace (among people and groups), and global peace (among nations), and peace with nature.
Johan Galtung, the founder of peace studies, distinguished between negative and positive peace and identified direct, structural and cultural violence.
Peace is necessary for human security, development, cooperation and healthy social life. Education can develop attitudes and skills that support peaceful living.

The world faces wars, terrorism, communal violence, ethnic conflicts, domestic violence and bullying in schools. Peace is necessary for protecting human life, economic development, democracy, human rights and environmental sustainability.

The UNESCO Constitution states, 'Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.' Hence education has a vital role in building a culture of peace.
Positive peace refers to the presence of justice, cooperation and conditions that reduce structural causes of violence.

Positive peace, as explained by Johan Galtung, is the absence of structural violence - social injustice, poverty, discrimination and exploitation - and the presence of social justice, equality, human rights and cooperation.
It is long-lasting because it removes the root causes of conflict. Education promotes positive peace by teaching justice, equality, tolerance and respect for human rights.
Negative peace means the absence of direct violence or open conflict.
Negative peace is the absence of war, physical violence and open conflict, often maintained through ceasefires, police, military power or treaties.
It is necessary but not sufficient, because underlying injustices may still exist and conflict can return. For lasting peace, negative peace should be transformed into positive peace.

The syllabus includes theories emphasizing healthy relationships, individual change, political elites, economics, root causes and justice, reduction of violence, withdrawal of resources for war, grassroots mobilisation and public attitudes.

Some important theories of change in peacebuilding are: (1) healthy relationships and connections theory - peace develops through dialogue and relationship-building; (2) individual change theory - peace comes through changes in individuals' attitudes and skills; (3) political elites theory - peace depends on changing the attitudes and interests of leaders; (4) economic theory - economic development and fair distribution reduce conflict; (5) root causes/justice theory - addressing injustice and inequality ensures peace.
Others include the withdrawal of resources for war theory and the reduction of violence theory. Each theory suggests different strategies, and education can contribute to all of them.
The five approaches listed in the syllabus are power politics, world order, conflict resolution, nonviolence and transformation.

According to peace educator Ian Harris and others: (1) power politics paradigm - peace through strength and balance of power; (2) world order paradigm - peace through international institutions and law (like the UN); (3) conflict resolution paradigm - peace through negotiation, mediation and communication; (4) nonviolence paradigm - peace through nonviolent action, as practised by Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.; (5) transformation paradigm - peace through transforming individuals and social structures.
These paradigms show that peace can be pursued at personal, social, national and international levels.
Peace Education develops knowledge, values, attitudes and skills for peaceful relationships, non-violence and constructive handling of conflict.

UNICEF defines peace education as the process of promoting the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values needed to bring about behaviour changes that will enable people to prevent conflict and violence, resolve conflict peacefully, and create conditions conducive to peace.

Components include human rights education, conflict resolution education, global education, environmental education, development education and education for nonviolence. NCF 2005 included 'Education for Peace' as a national focus area.

sections.title: Origin and Aims of Peace Education

blocks.text: Peace Education developed from wider efforts to prevent violence and promote peaceful societies. Its aims include cooperation, tolerance, justice and conflict-resolution skills.

Origin: Peace education grew after World War I and especially after World War II, inspired by thinkers like Maria Montessori, John Dewey, Gandhi and Tagore. UNESCO, the UN International Decade for a Culture of Peace and Non-violence (2001-2010) and international peace movements supported it.

Aims: developing inner peace and self-control, promoting tolerance and respect for diversity, teaching nonviolent conflict resolution, promoting human rights and justice, developing global citizenship and protecting the environment.

sections.title: Need for Peace in Human Life

blocks.text: Peace supports personal well-being, stable relationships, social cooperation and development.

Peace in individual life brings mental health, happiness and better learning. Peace in the family and community creates harmonious relationships and cooperation. Peace in the nation allows democracy, development and national integration, while global peace prevents war and supports international cooperation.
Without peace, resources are wasted on conflicts, human rights are violated and development is blocked. Thus peace is a basic human need and a precondition for sustainable development.
Peace Education can focus on areas such as non-violence, human rights, conflict resolution, cooperation and development of peaceful values.

Types of peace education include: (1) international education - understanding other cultures and global issues; (2) human rights education; (3) conflict resolution education; (4) development education - poverty, justice and equity; (5) environmental education; (6) education for nonviolence; (7) multicultural education.
It may be formal (through the curriculum), non-formal (community programmes and NGOs) or informal (family and media).
Education can promote peace through values, dialogue, tolerance, cooperation, respect for diversity and non-violent problem-solving.

Strategies: integrating peace themes into subjects like history, literature and social science; co-curricular activities such as debates, dramas, peace clubs and celebration of International Day of Peace (21 September); cooperative learning; mediation programmes; and a democratic school climate.

Teachers play a key role by modelling peaceful behaviour, avoiding corporal punishment, treating all students equally, encouraging dialogue and teaching life skills such as empathy, communication and anger management.
Conflict is a situation of opposition or incompatibility between needs, interests, values, goals or perceptions.

Conflict is a natural part of human life. It can be constructive (leading to growth, innovation and better relationships) or destructive (leading to violence and breakdown of relationships), depending on how it is handled.
Stages of conflict include latent conflict, perceived conflict, felt conflict, manifest conflict and conflict aftermath (Pondy's model). Understanding conflict helps in managing it effectively.
Intrapersonal conflict occurs within an individual, such as conflict between competing goals or choices.

Kurt Lewin classified intrapersonal conflicts into: approach-approach conflict (choosing between two attractive options, e.g. two good colleges), avoidance-avoidance conflict (choosing between two undesirable options), and approach-avoidance conflict (one goal with both positive and negative features). Multiple approach-avoidance conflicts also occur.
Such conflicts may cause stress, anxiety and frustration. Guidance, counselling and decision-making skills help students resolve them.
Interpersonal conflict occurs between individuals.

Interpersonal conflicts arise from differences in opinions, values, interests, personality, communication problems and competition for resources. Examples include conflicts between friends, classmates, siblings, or a teacher and a student.
They can be resolved through effective communication, listening, empathy, compromise, negotiation and mediation.
Intergroup conflict occurs between social groups.

Intergroup conflicts occur between groups such as castes, religious communities, ethnic groups, political parties, departments or student groups. Causes include competition for scarce resources, prejudice, stereotypes, historical grievances and identity politics.

Examples include communal riots and ethnic clashes. Strategies to reduce them include contact between groups, cooperative goals (superordinate goals as in Sherif's Robbers Cave experiment), dialogue and fair distribution of resources.
Inter-organizational conflict occurs between organisations.

Inter-organisational conflicts occur between organisations such as companies, trade unions and management, government departments, or nations. Causes include competition for resources, markets or power, differences in goals and policies, and contractual disputes.
They are resolved through negotiation, arbitration, mediation, legal processes and agreements.

The syllabus identifies information, miscommunication, resources, relationships, interests and needs, structures, power, governance, rights, culture, ideology, religion, identity and values as possible bases of conflict.

Explanation of bases: (1) information - lack of or different information; (2) miscommunication - misunderstandings; (3) resources - competition for scarce resources; (4) relationships - past grievances and mistrust; (5) interests and needs - incompatible goals; (6) structures - unequal power or unfair systems; (7) power - struggle for control; (8) governance - poor administration and corruption.
Other bases include rights (violation of human rights), cultural differences, values and identity, religion and ethnicity. Identifying the basis helps choose the right method of conflict resolution.
Conflict management uses methods to prevent escalation and handle disagreements constructively.

Thomas and Kilmann identified five conflict-handling styles: competing (assertive and uncooperative), accommodating (cooperative but unassertive), avoiding (neither), collaborating (both assertive and cooperative - win-win) and compromising (middle path).

Methods include negotiation, mediation (a neutral third party helps), arbitration (third party decides), dialogue, problem-solving and conciliation. Collaboration is often the best approach because it addresses everyone's needs.
Education develops communication, empathy, tolerance, negotiation and problem-solving skills that help people resolve conflict peacefully.
Education teaches life skills recommended by WHO, such as communication, empathy, critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making and managing emotions, which are useful for conflict resolution.

Schools can set up peer mediation programmes, use cooperative learning, teach about other cultures to reduce prejudice and create democratic classrooms. Teachers should model fair and respectful handling of disputes.

sections.title: Concept, Types and Significance of Peace

blocks.text:
Peace is not simply absence of war. Negative peace refers mainly to absence of direct violence, while positive peace includes justice, cooperation and social conditions that reduce causes of violence.

Peace is important for personal well-being, stable society and development. The syllabus presents several peace theories and five broad paradigms: power politics, world order, conflict resolution, nonviolence and transformation.

These approaches explain peace from different viewpoints, ranging from management of power to deeper transformation of relationships and structures.

Concept of peace: Peace is not only the absence of war but the presence of justice, harmony and well-being. Johan Galtung distinguished negative peace (absence of direct violence) and positive peace (absence of structural violence and presence of justice).

Need and significance: Peace is essential for life, development, democracy, human rights and environmental protection. Conflicts and violence cause loss of life, poverty and suffering. UNESCO emphasises that peace must be built in human minds through education.

Theories and paradigms: Theories of change emphasise relationships, individual change, political elites, economic development and justice. The five paradigms - power politics, world order, conflict resolution, nonviolence and transformation - show different paths to peace.
Conclusion: Lasting peace requires moving from negative peace to positive peace by addressing root causes of conflict, and education plays a central role in this transformation.

Peace Education develops knowledge, values, attitudes and skills needed for peaceful living. It encourages tolerance, cooperation, non-violence, justice and respect for others.

Its need arises because conflict and violence affect individuals and societies. Education can help learners understand differences, communicate respectfully and solve problems without violence.

The role of education is therefore both preventive and constructive: it develops peaceful attitudes and prepares learners to participate responsibly in society.
Meaning: Peace education develops knowledge, skills, attitudes and values for preventing and resolving conflicts peacefully and creating a just and peaceful society.

Origin and aims: It grew after the World Wars through the ideas of Montessori, Dewey, Gandhi and Tagore, and through UNESCO and UN initiatives. Its aims include inner peace, tolerance, respect for diversity, human rights, nonviolent conflict resolution and global citizenship.
Types: International education, human rights education, conflict resolution education, development education, environmental education and education for nonviolence.

Role of education: Schools can integrate peace themes into the curriculum, use cooperative learning, organise peace clubs and celebrations, create a democratic and non-violent school climate and teach life skills. Teachers act as role models of peaceful behaviour.

Conflict occurs when individuals or groups experience incompatible interests, needs, goals or values. It may be intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup or inter-organizational.

The syllabus identifies many possible bases of conflict, including poor information, miscommunication, resources, relationships, interests, structures, power, governance, rights, culture, ideology, religion, identity and values.

Understanding the source of a conflict is important because different causes require different methods of management.

Meaning and nature: Conflict is a situation in which individuals or groups have incompatible goals, interests or values. It is natural and can be constructive or destructive depending on how it is handled.

Types: Intrapersonal conflict occurs within a person (approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance); interpersonal conflict occurs between individuals; intergroup conflict between groups; and inter-organisational conflict between organisations.

Bases of conflict: Lack of information, miscommunication, competition for resources, poor relationships, incompatible interests and needs, unfair structures, power struggles, poor governance, violation of rights and cultural differences.
Importance: Understanding the type and basis of a conflict is the first step in managing it. Teachers who understand conflict can help students handle their own conflicts constructively.

sections.title: Conflict Management and Role of Education

blocks.text:
Conflict management aims to handle disagreements constructively and prevent unnecessary escalation. Useful approaches can involve communication, dialogue, negotiation, cooperation and problem-solving.

Education helps conflict resolution by developing empathy, critical thinking, tolerance and communication skills. It can also challenge prejudice and create opportunities for dialogue.

Peace Education therefore prepares learners not merely to avoid conflict but to respond to it in responsible and non-violent ways.

Conflict management: Conflict management aims to reduce negative effects and increase positive outcomes of conflict. The Thomas-Kilmann model identifies competing, accommodating, avoiding, compromising and collaborating styles, with collaboration giving win-win outcomes.
Methods: Negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dialogue, problem-solving and reconciliation are common methods. Nonviolent methods inspired by Gandhi are also important.

Role of education: Education develops communication, empathy, tolerance, critical thinking and negotiation skills. Schools can promote peer mediation, cooperative learning, inclusive curricula and value education that reduce prejudice and violence.
Conclusion: By teaching students to resolve conflicts peacefully, education builds a foundation for a peaceful society and nation.
